title: Straighten: A Place for Everything
subtitle: The second S. Sorting decided what stays; now give every keeper one clear home, so that putting it back is easier than putting it down anywhere else.
part_position: First chapter of Part Four (Straighten), chapters 12 to 15; this chapter opens Straighten and begins the second of the six S's
follows: Chapter 11 (What to Donate, Sell, Store, Recycle, or Throw Away)
hands_off_note: Chapter 13 keeps working inside Straighten: every keeper has a home now, but not every home is in the best spot yet, so the next chapter places the daily things within quick reach and the rare things a step out of the way.
audience: Readers who have just finished Sort and are standing over a cleared surface that holds only its keepers, each still sitting loose where it landed with no place of its own. Busy home keepers and parents. Applying the method, not new to it. They do not need to decide what stays again; they need to give each thing that stayed one clear home so the surface holds without a nightly tidy.
core_promise: Open the second S by giving every keeper one clear home, a single spot where it lives and returns to, and judge each home by one plain test, that putting the thing back is easier than putting it down anywhere else and takes no more than one easy motion. Reframe the failure to put things away as a design problem, a missing or bad home, not a character flaw, then walk the entryway keepers into homes one by one so the surface stays clear on its own.
emotional_purpose: Lift the shame that clings to a messy surface. You were never messy; your things simply had nowhere to go. Make the second S feel light, closer to carpentry than to soul-searching, because giving a thing a home asks almost nothing of you emotionally after the harder work of Sort. Deliver the honest first-Straighten-step milestone without overselling it: the room got easier even though nothing left the house.
practical_purpose: Draw the line between deciding a thing stays (already done in Sort) and deciding where it lives (today's only job); state the core principle that a place for everything is what lets everything find its way back; teach the Home Test as the one tool that separates a good home from a bad one; explain why things do not get put away (the home is too far or too much work, not the person); walk the entryway keepers into homes one at a time, keys to a tray or hook, leash to a hook, umbrella to a stand or hook, bag to a hook, mail to an outgoing slot; and read the friction meter as the first Straighten step past the Sort-complete milestone.
primary_cta: Pick the one thing you use every day and reach for most, and give it a single home within arm's reach of where you use it. Return it there for three days and watch how fast putting it back stops being a decision. Read the chapter free in the online book.
secondary_cta: Read the chapter free online, then continue to Chapter 13, where Straighten keeps working: every keeper has a home now, but not every home is in the best spot yet, so the next chapter puts the daily things within quick reach and the rare things a little out of the way.

secondary_device: The core principle, a place for everything so everything can find its way back, paired with the anti-shame reframe that the failure to put things away is a design problem (a missing or bad home), not a character flaw; every home is judged by the one-easy-motion return

worked_example.space: the entryway console after Sort, holding only its five keepers sitting loose where they landed, each given one home judged by the Home Test
worked_example.note: Every home landed within reach of the door, because that is where these things are used and let go. None of the homes is clever and none needs a special product; each was chosen for one reason only, that returning the thing there is a single easy motion, so the console stays clear on its own without a nightly tidy.

items.keys: A small tray on the console or a hook at the door, positioned so the hand coming in drops or hangs them in the same motion it uses to close the door; dropping them there beats setting them on the nearest surface, so it passes the test.
items.leash: One hook by the door, grabbed on the way out and hung on the way back, no drawer to open and no tangle to fish through, so it survives constant use and passes on both legs of the trip.
items.umbrella: A stand or a hook right at the door, not the back of a hall closet; a home you have to open a door and reach past three coats to use fails the test, so put it where you actually pass on your way out.
items.reusable_bag: A hook, ideally right beside the leash, so it is hanging there when you leave and back in a single motion when you return, instead of migrating to the car or the bottom of another bag.
items.tomorrows_mail: One small outgoing tray or slot right by the door, a launching place rather than a resting one, so the letter to post or form to return rides out in your hand the next time you leave rather than sinking into a pile.

worked_example.tally: All five keepers got a home within reach of the door, each judged by one easy motion of return. Nothing left the house, yet the surface is now clear in a way that holds, because putting each thing back is finally the path of least resistance instead of an extra chore.

definition: Straighten, the second S, gives every keeper one clear home, a single spot where it lives and returns to. A place for everything, and everything in its place, so the space stays easy without effort.
one_idea_to_keep: Tidy is not a chore you repeat forever. It is a set of homes good enough that things find their own way back. Build the homes once, and the room helps keep itself.
key_motifs: the first chapter of Part Four (Straighten); it opens the second of the six S's and makes the turn from removing to arranging
an arranging chapter, not a removing one: deciding a thing stays and deciding where it lives are two separate acts, and Sort only did the first
the keepers were left exactly where the Sort pass dropped them, sitting loose with no places of their own; a keeper with nowhere to go is just tomorrow's clutter arriving early
the core principle: a place for everything, so everything can find its way back; the point of a home is the return trip
Straighten asks almost nothing of you emotionally; it is closer to carpentry than to soul-searching
why things do not get put away is a design answer, not a character one: the home is too far, behind a door, under a lid, or never decided
the anti-shame reframe: you were never messy, your things simply had nowhere to go; the problem was never your willpower, it was the design
the Home Test: a home works when putting the thing back is easier than putting it down anywhere else, and takes no more than one easy motion
the best homes are the ones you never notice yourself using, because the return is folded into a motion you were already making
the entryway worked example: keys to a tray or hook, leash to a hook, umbrella to a stand or hook, bag to a hook, mail to an outgoing slot, every home within reach of the door
a room that helps keep itself: you did not become tidier, you built small homes that do the tidying that used to fall to you
the fences: do not re-open Sort, do not yet place homes by frequency of use (Chapter 13), add labels or visual controls (Chapter 14), or map the whole room (Chapter 15)
Straighten is the English name for seiton, a place for everything and everything in its place, referenced lightly and home-scaled
